summary: A seven-day culinary & wine tour itinerary in Vilnius, Aukštaitija (northeast Lithuania), Biržai, Dzūkija, Lithuania.

itinerary.title: Vilnius: the old town table
itinerary.morning: Arrive Vilnius. The old town is the largest surviving baroque old town in Eastern Europe, on the UNESCO list, and walkable end to end in forty minutes.
itinerary.afternoon: **Halės Turgus**, the covered market since 1906: rye bread, smoked meats, curd cheese, forest mushrooms and honey. Lunch here. Then Užupis, the self-declared artists' republic across the Vilnia river with its own constitution on a wall in thirty languages.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at one of the restaurants reinterpreting Lithuanian historical cuisine, the Grand Duchy's kitchen, with its game, rye and preserved fruit, is being seriously researched and cooked in Vilnius right now. `verify: true`

itinerary.title: Vilnius: beer bars and the modern kitchen
itinerary.morning: The Gediminas Tower and the Palace of the Grand Dukes for the context that explains the food: this was the capital of a state that stretched to the Black Sea.
itinerary.afternoon: Vilnius's **farmhouse-beer bars** are the point of this day. A handful of small bars in the old town and in Naujamiestis serve rotating *kaimiškas alus* from named village brewers, often unfiltered, low-carbonation, and unlike anything in the German or Belgian traditions.
itinerary.evening: Snack culture: smoked pig ears, *kepta duona* (fried garlic rye), curd cheese and salted peas, which exist specifically to be eaten with farmhouse ale.

itinerary.title: Trakai and the Karaim kitchen
itinerary.morning: Trakai, 30 minutes west: the island castle on Lake Galvė, red brick on water, rebuilt in the 20th century and unmistakable.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Karaim** community, a Turkic people brought here in the 14th century by Grand Duke Vytautas, still lives on the town's main street in three-windowed wooden houses. Their **kibinai**, a baked pastry of lamb and onion, is one of the region's great dishes and is made properly only here.
itinerary.evening: Return to Vilnius, or drive north to start the Aukštaitija leg.

itinerary.title: Aukštaitija: the farmhouse brewing heartland
itinerary.morning: Drive north toward Panevėžys and Pasvalys (about 2 h). This is flat, fertile, barley country and the last place in Europe where farmhouse brewing survived without a revival, it simply never stopped.
itinerary.afternoon: Visit an actual farm brewery. **Jovarų Alus** is the most famous, brewed by hand in a village with equipment that looks agricultural because it is. Arrangements must be made ahead and a Lithuanian-speaking guide helps enormously.
itinerary.evening: Biržai, the beer capital: a castle, a lake, and two large regional breweries in town alongside the farm producers. Dinner with local ale and *skilandis*.

itinerary.title: Biržai karst, Anykščiai and the fruit wines
itinerary.morning: The **Kirkilai karst lakes** outside Biržai, a landscape of sinkholes where the gypsum bedrock collapses, with a viewing tower over dozens of small water-filled craters.
itinerary.afternoon: South to Anykščiai for the fruit-wine tradition, Lithuania's berry and apple wines are a serious regional industry, plus the treetop walkway in the Anykščiai pine forest and the narrow-gauge railway.

itinerary.title: Stakliškės mead and the Dzūkija forest
itinerary.morning: **Stakliškės**, south of Vilnius, is where Lithuanian mead is made to a documented traditional method, honey, water, hops and herbs, fermented and matured for months rather than fortified. The tasting explains why *midus* is closer to a wine than to the sweet mead most people expect.
itinerary.afternoon: Into **Dzūkija National Park**: pine forest, sand, and villages like Zervynos and Musteika, where the UNESCO-listed **tree-beekeeping** tradition is still practised, hives hollowed into living pines, worked with a rope and a climbing seat.
itinerary.evening: Mushrooms. Dzūkija is Lithuania's foraging heartland and in September the entire region is in the forest at dawn. A guesthouse dinner here will be built around what was picked that morning.

itinerary.title: Vilnius return and departure
itinerary.morning: Last market run at Halės or the Tymo market for honey, black bread, smoked cheese and a bottle of mead.
itinerary.afternoon: Vilnius airport is fifteen minutes from the old town.

accommodationStrategy.name: Vilnius old town boutique hotels
accommodationStrategy.description: Small hotels in restored baroque and 19th-century buildings, €80-150. Everything on Days 1-3 is walkable, which matters on a beer itinerary. Look for a property between the cathedral and Užupis.

accommodationStrategy.name: Biržai / Aukštaitija country guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: Simple, warm, and often with a sauna and a host who brews or knows who does. This is the region where the accommodation is the introduction, a guesthouse owner will get you into a farm brewery that no website lists.

accommodationStrategy.name: Dzūkija forest homesteads
accommodationStrategy.description: Wooden houses in pine forest near Merkinė or Marcinkonys, €50-90, with home cooking and mushroom knowledge. The right ending for the week and a completely different Lithuania from Vilnius.

logistics.emergency: 112. Vilnius has excellent hospitals; rural Aukštaitija and Dzūkija are 40-90 minutes from one.
logistics.bookingWindows: Vilnius restaurants: 1-3 weeks. Brewery visits: 2-4 weeks via a guide. Guesthouses in mushroom season: 3-4 weeks, and note that September weekends in Dzūkija are busy with Lithuanian foragers.

other.label: Farmhouse breweries are farms
other.text: They are not visitor centres, several do not have websites, and the brewer may speak only Lithuanian. Either go with a specialist beer guide from Vilnius or have your guesthouse arrange it. Turning up unannounced is not the custom. `verify: true`

other.label: What farmhouse ale is
other.text: Often unboiled or briefly boiled wort, family yeast cultures, farm-grown hops, low carbonation, served fresh and sometimes cloudy. Shelf life is short and it does not travel, which is precisely why you go to it.

other.label: Alcohol law
other.text: Lithuania has some of the EU's strictest alcohol regulation: a **0.0‰ drink-drive limit for drivers with under two years' experience and 0.4‰ otherwise**, retail sale restricted by hour, and a minimum purchase age of 20. Plan drivers accordingly. `verify: true`

other.label: Foraging
other.text: Mushroom and berry picking on public forest land is legal and is a national obsession. Do not pick in strict nature reserves, and never eat anything a local has not confirmed, Lithuania has genuinely dangerous lookalikes.

other.label: Driving
other.text: Good roads, headlights on at all times, winter tyres compulsory 10 November-1 April. Rural drink-driving enforcement is strict and checkpoints are common.

proTips: Hire a **specialist beer guide** for the Aukštaitija day. It costs less than a good dinner and it is the difference between drinking farmhouse ale in a Vilnius bar and drinking it out of the fermenter with the man who made it.

Ask for the **beer snack menu** (*užkandžiai*) rather than a main course. Smoked pig ears, fried rye with garlic, salted peas, curd cheese and dried meat is the correct meal with farmhouse ale and it costs €10.

**Šaltibarščiai**, the neon-pink cold beetroot and kefir soup with hot potatoes on the side, is a summer-only dish and Lithuanians are passionate about it. Order it any time between May and September.
Mead from **Stakliškės** is the single best thing to bring home from this trip: it is unlike commercial mead, it ages, and it is difficult to find outside the country.
Go in **late September**. Mushroom season, honey harvest, apple wine, warm days and beer festivals in the Aukštaitija towns all coincide.

Vilnius's food scene has changed dramatically in the last decade and the historical-cuisine research movement is the most interesting thing happening in Baltic food. Book one such dinner deliberately, early in the week, it frames everything you eat afterwards.

raw.appellations_and_terroir: Not a wine country, this is Europe's last living **farmhouse ale** tradition, plus honey. Lithuanian *kaimiškas alus* uses raw or lightly boiled wort, local landrace yeasts kept in families for generations, and hops grown on the farm. Stakliškės mead is made to a documented traditional recipe; Lithuanian and Polish **tree beekeeping** was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2020
